p.title: Mapping Political Communities: A Statistical Analysis of Lobbying Networks in Legislative Politics

ext.title: Mapping Political Communities: A Statistical Analysis of Lobbying Networks in Legislative Politics
ext.venue: Political Analysis (Cambridge University Press, for the Society for Political Methodology)
ext.document_type: Peer-reviewed journal article: methods paper with an empirical application
ext.coverage: Full main text read in chunks (text file lines 0-1066 = journal pp. 1-20 through the bibliography; nothing left unread). NOT in the supplied text and not read: Appendices A-E, Figures F.1-F.5, Stan code (Appendix C), permutation-test details (B.2), assortativity (D.2), alignment (E). Metadata hint corrected: the hint left year, venue and DOI blank and wrote authors as 'Kim, Kunisky'. The paper is 2020, Political Analysis, DOI 10.1017/pan.2020.29, by In Song Kim and Dmitriy Kunisky. Annotations: both JSON files read in full. edb70a4800ee.json holds about 117 highlights (pp. 1-18). 0d56770b8d81.json holds about 50 highlights (pp. 1-18) that largely duplicate the first set; its entries are listed after the first set in paul_markup. All are highlights by Paul Goff with empty note fields, so there are no sticky-note comments in either file. Colours: yellow/orange for most, green for some, purple for replication and data sentences on p. 3. Covered text is verbatim as extracted, trimmed to 40 words where longer. Equation blocks and garbled extractions are marked in brackets rather than reproduced. The paper's empirical section uses one Congress (113th); the lobbying database spans 1999-2017.
ext.research_question: How can latent memberships of political actors in the communities that drive their observable interactions be inferred, when the network is bipartite, actors hold several memberships, and a pair of actors can interact in several ways? Application: which legislation communities organize interest-group lobbying of legislators in the 113th Congress, and when do domain-specific groups lobby outside their domain?
ext.theory: Interest-group influence runs through repeated, narrow issue ties. Lobbying is organised into legislation communities that group interest groups with the legislators who hold relevant jurisdiction (e.g. Energy, Veterans' Affairs). Actors can have mixed memberships, because groups with broad interests and politicians with broad roles span several communities. A pair can also have mixed interactions, since one dyad's bills can belong to different issue communities. Industry-specific interests are the primary driver of lobbying; other motives play at most a secondary role. Social issues (the 'Civil Society' community) are the one broad cross-industry domain (pp. 10-11, 17). Power committees (Ways and Means, Appropriations) carry high-entropy politicians (p. 10). Anomalous dyads with more interactions than predicted suggest geography, campaign-contribution ties, or bill-specific stakes (p. 11). The model is motivated by the biSBM and mmSBM literatures (pp. 3-5).
ext.data: Lobbying reports: 1,111,859 reports filed 1999-2017, yielding 2,396,693 issue corpora, 20,092 special interest groups and 1,164 current or former members of Congress (p. 7). Bills: 108,086 bills introduced in the 106th-114th Congresses were identified by NLP on lobbying reports (p. 2). About 12,000 bills are introduced per Congress, and most are lobbied by at least one group (Figure 2, p. 7). Analysis sample: the 113th Congress network. Unit: interest group i by politician j dyad, with A_ij = number of bills group i lobbied that politician j sponsored (p. 7). The main text does not state the 113th-Congress N of groups and politicians. Lobbied-bill distribution in the 113th Congress: median 3 groups per bill, maximum 946 (H.R. 1), and 23% of lobbied bills have one lobbying group (Figure 2 caption, p. 7). Session identification for bill references used report text signals, bill-text similarity, and 'Act of [YEAR]' phrases (p. 7).
ext.method: Bipartite Link Community Model (biLCM): A_ij ~ Poisson(sum over z of kappa_z * alpha_iz * beta_jz), with z = 1..k link communities (eq. 1, p. 5). Estimation by EM with ancillary parameters q_ij(z) (eqs. 2-5, p. 6). Normalisation: sum_i alpha_iz = sum_j beta_jz = 1 for each z. k = 8 communities, chosen with reference to community structure seen in the latent space model (fn. 11). 50 random starts; highest likelihood kept (p. 6). Membership shares p_iz and q_jz are normalised kappa_z-weighted alphas and betas; entropy H in bits, with about 2^H communities actively used (p. 9). Comparison models: (a) 2-D latent space model with Poisson mean exp(alpha_i + beta_j - ||theta_i - psi_j||^2), Bayesian in Stan with hierarchical priors (eq. 6, pp. 12-13); (b) degree-corrected bipartite SBM (dc-biSBM), EM from Larremore et al. (2014), k = l = 8, 50 starts (eq. 7, pp. 15-16). Significance: permutation test against a null that keeps actor-level activity distributions (p. 12). Anomalies: observed versus biLCM-estimated counts, ranked by deviation (Table 1, p. 11).
ext.identification: Not causal. The model is identified by the normalisation constraints on alpha and beta. Communities are latent structure inferred from co-lobbying counts; the paper makes no treatment-effect identification claim. Community names and committee matches are the authors' judgement from the leading groups in each community (p. 7).
ext.scope: Population: interest groups and members of Congress who co-appear through lobbying disclosures (1999-2017 database), with the empirical application restricted to the 113th Congress (2013-2014). Institution: US Congress and federal lobbying disclosure. Era: 1999-2017 data; 113th Congress for estimates. The method is general to bipartite networks with mixed memberships; Section 3.4 (pp. 17-18) lists proposed uses in patronage networks, voter-politician contributions, roll-call ideal points and global value chains, none tested in the paper.

key_findings.finding: Eight legislation communities are named by their leading groups: Healthcare, Veterans' Affairs, Technology & Telecommunications, Energy, Finance & Insurance, Universities & Research, Civil Society, and Retail & Transportation.
key_findings.location: p. 7, paragraph 'We name the legislation communities'

key_findings.finding: Specialist groups lobby a single community; generalists spread across several. MICROSOFT and ARCH COAL interact with one community at probability of at least 85%. MCAFEE interacts with Technology & Telecom at 31% and Universities & Research at 52%. PHILIPS NORTH AMERICA and the CHAMBER OF COMMERCE have no single community above 25%.
key_findings.numbers: MICROSOFT, ARCH COAL: at least 85% in one community; MCAFEE: 31% and 52%; PHILIPS and CHAMBER: at most 25% per community

key_findings.finding: Specialist and generalist interest groups coexist. Targeted groups lobby committees with narrow jurisdiction; broad groups target power committees (Ways and Means, Senate Appropriations).
key_findings.numbers: not stated as a single statistic

key_findings.finding: Only one broad issue area is lobbied by diverse groups: Civil Society, covering social and human-rights legislation. It is the fourth most active of eight communities by kappa_z, so it accounts for only a modest share of lobbying activity.
Politicians with high entropy, meaning membership in at least four communities, sit on power committees such as Ways and Means and Senate Appropriations, which control the power of the purse.
key_findings.numbers: entropy at least 2 corresponds to at least 4 communities; 52% of the 113th Congress were Republican (Figure 4 caption)

key_findings.finding: Politicians interacting with a community at probability at least 40% sit on committees matching its subject (e.g. Financial Services for Finance & Insurance; Armed Services for the defence-related group).

Anomalous dyads (observed far above biLCM prediction) are explained by geography, campaign contributions, or bill-specific stakes rather than shared issues. Examples: Tom Marino-CVS 10 observed vs 0.55 expected; Michael Enzi-eBay 11 vs 1.08; Jeanne Shaheen-Novo Nordisk 12 vs 1.61; Mike Conaway-iHeartMedia 7 vs 0.17.
key_findings.numbers: 10 dyads listed; largest gap Shaheen-Novo Nordisk 12 observed vs 1.61 estimated

key_findings.finding: Community structure is significant. In the permutation null (networks with the same actor-activity distributions), interest groups have much higher numbers of community memberships than in the observed network, so the observed network has strong community structure.
key_findings.numbers: not quantified in the main text (test details in Appendix B.2, not read)

key_findings.finding: The 2-D latent space model finds the same single-community clusters (e.g. Technology adjacent to Telecom and Energy; Universities adjacent to Industrial Research and Healthcare). Actors with mixed memberships fall in the centre of the latent space, where the LSM is uninformative. The paper attributes this to stochastic-equivalence confounding (Minhas et al. 2019).
key_findings.numbers: 2-D LSM; high-entropy hexagons cluster near the centre

key_findings.finding: The dc-biSBM recovers community boundaries that match the LSM clusters, and it finds two central communities (Civil Society and Retail & Transportation). It still assigns each actor to one community, so it misses mixed memberships. Chamber of Commerce, BP and McAfee fall in overlaps of community pairs.

The biLCM is proposed as a general tool: for ideal-point estimation from roll calls treated as bipartite networks, for patronage and campaign-contribution networks, and for allocation of intermediate products in global value chains. These are proposed uses, not tested in the paper.

limitations: The number of communities k must be chosen in advance; the paper calls for model selection or a Dirichlet-process prior (p. 17).
No covariates are used, though rich politician and group data exist (p. 17).
The model handles two-mode networks only; multi-partite interactions (group, politician, bill) are left to future work, e.g. tensor regression (pp. 17-18).
The data do not distinguish lobbying for from lobbying against a bill (p. 10), so alignment is inferred from co-lobbying only.
Lobbying reports do not name the politicians contacted; the network is built indirectly from sponsored bills (pp. 6-7).
Bill identification by NLP is error-prone, and session identification for bills referenced only by number is hard; the paper cites OpenSecrets misattributions (fn. 8, p. 7).
EM is not guaranteed to reach the global maximum, so the paper uses 50 random starts (pp. 6, 16).
The empirical application uses one Congress (113th); cross-session comparison is preliminary (fn. 5; Appendix B.3).
Anomaly explanations (geography, contributions, bill salience) are offered as suggestive and are not tested (p. 11).

Entropy threshold: H at least 2 means at least four communities (p. 10)

rel.summary_md:
Kim and Kunisky propose the Bipartite Link Community Model (biLCM). It is a Poisson model of a two-mode count matrix in which each interaction between an interest group and a politician is assigned to one of k latent "link communities". This allows mixed memberships, where an actor belongs to several communities, and mixed interactions, where one pair interacts in several communities. The model is fitted by EM with 50 random starts and k = 8. The application covers the 113th Congress only. A_ij counts the bills that group i lobbied and politician j sponsored, so the network is built indirectly because LD-2 reports never name the members contacted. The paper finds eight legislation communities that match committee jurisdictions. Specialists (MICROSOFT and ARCH COAL, at least 85% in one community) coexist with generalists (the CHAMBER OF COMMERCE, no community above 25%). Generalists and senior leaders cluster on power committees. Civil Society is the only cross-industry domain. The paper concludes that narrow industry interest drives most lobbying. A latent space model and a dc-biSBM recover the same blocks but miss mixed membership.

For Paul's systems, the most direct point is this. The paper's lobbying network uses the same construction as Melange's lobbied-member link: an organisation is credited to a member through a bill roster. The paper never treats that link as contact or influence, which backs the system's ruling that the link is circular. Three other bearings qualify claims the system makes. First, the dashboard cites the paper for "exploitable community structure" in the cosponsor graph, but the paper's communities are group-by-member lobbying communities, and budgetRecruit has no community term. Second, co-lobbying cannot separate lobbying for a bill from lobbying against it, so the paper cannot identify rival-industry champions. Third, leaders' broad memberships show how widely they draw lobbying, not leverage on credit-union issues. Everything here is descriptive, comes from one Congress, and is not causal.

bearings.paper_claim: Lobbying reports do not name the politicians contacted, so the network is built indirectly: A_ij = number of bills group i lobbied that politician j sponsored. The resulting communities are read as co-attention structure, never as contact or influence. Window: 113th Congress; denominator: lobbied bills with an identified sponsor.
bearings.paper_location: pp. 6-7 (data construction; 'organizations need not identify their political contacts'); p. 10 (no for/against distinction)
bearings.system_side: The system builds client x bioguide x year counts by crediting every sponsor AND cosponsor of each lobbied bill (63,991 member-years). The brain records this link as circular: P(joined | lobbied) = 1 by construction, so it is refuted as influence evidence.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Carries over directly, since the construction is the same and the system's version is broader (it adds cosponsors). The paper avoids circularity only because it makes no claim that lobbying predicts sponsorship. Any reuse in Melange must likewise stay descriptive. Under D-021 the matrix is an identity source and cannot become an edge or weight source. The paper uses sponsors only, so its A_ij is not identical to the system's dyads.

bearings.paper_claim: Communities are latent memberships in the bipartite interest-group x politician lobbying network (k = 8, 113th Congress). The central finding is that hard partitions miss mixed memberships: senior members and party leaders typically span at least 4 communities (entropy at least 2), and the LSM and dc-biSBM misplace these mixed actors.
bearings.paper_location: pp. 8-10 (Figures 3-4, entropy); pp. 12-16 (LSM and dc-biSBM comparison)
bearings.system_side: The grounding comment and the brain note cite Kim-Kunisky for 'the cosponsor network has real community structure the pathfinder exploits'. budgetRecruit is a max-coverage greedy over member-member cosponsor edges with Noisy-OR coverage and degree pruning. It contains no community detection or community term.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper does not carry over as cited. Its communities belong to a different graph (organisation-member lobbying, not member-member cosponsorship), and the code does not use communities at all. The citation should be removed or re-scoped. If a community-local recruitment term is ever added, the paper argues for mixed membership over a hard Louvain-style partition, because hub members are exactly the ones a partition misassigns.

bearings.paper_claim: Politicians who interact with a community at probability at least 40% sit on committees with matching jurisdiction (e.g. Financial Services for Finance & Insurance). Broad, generalist groups target power committees (Ways and Means, Senate Appropriations) instead. Window: 113th Congress; lobbying-attention counts, not outcomes.
bearings.paper_location: p. 10 (Figure 4 and committee analysis); p. 2 intro
bearings.system_side: Committee% = (Membership + Leadership)/2 / max, with seat weights set by owner-judged CU-relevance tier (Highly 3.0, Moderately 1.8, Slightly 0.9). The pillar assumes jurisdictional seats carry structural CU power.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Supports the premise that lobbying attention is organised by jurisdiction, so CU-relevant seats are where finance lobbying lands. It does not show that seats produce CU outcomes. Evidence is from one Congress, federal, and a different era from the 119th. The power-committee finding suggests checking how tax-writing and appropriations seats (CU tax status) are tiered; their tiers were not verified here.

bearings.paper_claim: Finance & Insurance emerges as a single legislation community. Because lobbying data do not distinguish lobbying for from lobbying against a bill, co-lobbying places rival interests together.
bearings.paper_location: p. 7 (community naming); p. 10 ('data do not distinguish between lobbying for or against')
bearings.system_side: Separate CU, bank, crypto and fintech boards, with a crown law that bars a Tier-1 champion from any sector's threat board. Industry rivalry is encoded through signed tensor valence and opposition priors.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The biLCM cannot supply the rival-industry champions Paul's margin note asks for. It would merge banks and CUs into one community. Separating conflicting industries needs a signed position source (Kim J. et al. 2025), not co-lobbying structure. The paper neither supports nor refutes the crown law; it marks a limit of this method.

bearings.paper_claim: The legislators with the most community memberships are often senior politicians or party leaders. High-entropy members (at least 4 communities) sit on power committees. This is breadth of lobbying attention, not issue-specific leverage.
bearings.system_side: Hand-set constants treat leadership as CU leverage: committee leadership Chair 1.0 to Member 0.2, and party leadership Speaker 1.0 to Minority Whip 0.2.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper shows that leaders attract lobbying across many domains, so any one industry's share of their attention is diluted. That supports scoring leadership as general reach, not as CU-specific leverage. It says nothing about effectiveness on CU bills. Evidence covers one Congress and is descriptive.

bearings.paper_claim: Sector communities (Finance & Insurance, Technology & Telecom, Energy and others) can be inferred from organisation x member lobbying counts rather than defined in advance. A permutation null that keeps actor activity distributions shows the community structure is real.
bearings.system_side: Sector networks (bank_reg, crypto, CU) are member-member cosponsor graphs over hand-defined sector bill universes.
bearings.transfer_conditions: A biLCM fitted to the existing org x bioguide counts could serve as a descriptive check on whether the hand-drawn sector boundaries show up in lobbying. It could only be a diagnostic. Under D-021 its outputs must not become edges or weights, and the result stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Dyads with far more interactions than the biLCM predicts are suggestively explained by geography, campaign-contribution ties or bill-specific stakes. Examples: Shaheen-Novo Nordisk 12 observed vs 1.61 expected; Marino-CVS 10 vs 0.55. The paper does not test these explanations.
bearings.system_side: The bridge test related FEC giving to change in the LDA network. Round 3 found a raw rho of +0.153 and a four-control partial of -0.0002, and the test was closed pending a new vintage.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This suggests a different design: test whether FEC money concentrates on dyads with positive community-model residuals, rather than correlating levels. It is a hypothesis only. The paper offers anecdotes from one Congress. Residuals built on a bill-roster join inherit its circularity for any join outcome.

gaps_exposed: No mixed-membership or overlapping community model exists anywhere in the member SNA. Press HCoI uses Louvain hard partitions, which the paper shows misassign exactly the high-entropy hub members (leaders, power-committee members).

The org x member lobbying count matrix (lob_id, bioguide_id, year, n_bills) already exists but has no actor-activity-preserving null model. Any structure read from it is untested against a degree-preserving permutation baseline like the paper's.

The system has no residual or anomaly view: nothing flags organisation-member dyads that are unusually dense relative to issue alignment. These dyads are where the paper locates 'genuinely significant political connections' versus routine jurisdictional alignment.

No for/against signal attaches to LDA dyads (position ships empty, position_basis='not_disclosed'), so rival-industry structure cannot be read from lobbying co-attention. That needs a signed position source.
flags: CITATION MIS-TRANSFER: the dashboard's budget-mode grounding and the brain note in melange-dashboard-june-capstone cite Kim-Kunisky for exploitable community structure in the COSPONSOR network. The paper studies the bipartite lobbying network, and budgetRecruit (make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:779-795) uses no community term. The citation overstates the grounding.

D-021: the paper's core object is an LDA-derived group x politician network. Any proposal to fit a biLCM and feed its memberships or dyad intensities into kernels, edges or weights would breach D-021. Diagnostic and descriptive use only.

Circularity: the paper's A_ij uses the same bill-roster join as the refuted lobbied-member link. Nothing in the paper licenses reading lobbied-to-sponsored co-occurrence as contact or influence, and the paper itself does not.

Not a rejected-SNA argument: the paper uses sponsors only and models actor activity through degree terms (kappa x alpha x beta, dc-biSBM). Neither is an argument to drop regular cosponsorship edges or to apply per-edge volume normalisation to the member graph, so neither rejected proposal should be read into it.

Window and denominator: every figure in the paper covers the 113th Congress (2013-14), with bills identified by NLP from 1999-2017 LDA reports. Do not quote its shares (85%, 25%, 40%) as properties of the 119th Congress or of CU lobbying.
rel.paul_alignment: Partly aligned. Paul reads Kim and Kunisky as a tool for identifying champions (lobbied-member-link and industry-boards-crown). The paper does not support that reading. It measures shared co-lobbying attention, not alignment or contact, and its finance community would merge banks and CUs, so it cannot find rival-industry champions. His note is stale relative to the system: the system has since ruled the same bill-roster construction circular (P(joined | lobbied) = 1), which the notes do not reflect. His committee-pillar citation (money and lobbying concentrate in jurisdictional committees) is supported by the 40%-threshold committee-matching result. His leadership citation is supported as breadth, not leverage. His path-finding gap, turning bipartite lobbying data into a graph path-finding can run on, is real, but the dashboard's current Kim-Kunisky citation for budget mode claims more grounding than the code uses. No annotation was recorded in his takeaways for this work.

related.why: The biLCM network is distilled from the LobbyView bill-level lobbying database (Kim 2018). It shares that NLP bill-identification pipeline and its misattribution risks.
It supplies the signed bill positions (support, oppose, engage) that Kim-Kunisky lack. Without such positions, co-lobbying cannot separate rival industries.
Committee community structure in the House; Kim-Kunisky match their lobbying communities to the same committee jurisdictions. Both are cited together in the dashboard's grounding.
It extends lobbying-network analysis over time with issue codes, where Kim-Kunisky give a single-Congress snapshot and leave cross-session comparison preliminary.
It takes a multi-partite (hypergraph) approach to a lobby network, which addresses the group-politician-bill limitation Kim-Kunisky leave to tensor methods.
It uses signed partitioning of the legislator network. That supplies the sign that Kim-Kunisky's unsigned co-lobbying lacks, but it is still a hard partition without mixed membership.

paul_entries.text:
Kim, In Song, and Dmitriy Kunisky. “Mapping political communities: A statistical analysis of lobbying networks in Legislative Politics.” Political Analysis, vol. 29, no. 3, 23 Nov. 2020, pp. 317–336, https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2020.29.

This article by MIT professors In Song Kim and Dimitriy Kuinsky applies the theory of Social Network Analysis to the lobbying industry and members of Congress, using a novel Bipartite Link Community Model that captures mixed membership and representative congestion within an MOC. On the topic of “mixed interactions observed between actors,” what this means specifically is that, within the model, one can see that different interactions between the same two actors as a result of one of the actors, such as the Chamber of Commerce, taking on multiple, each distinct, issues. Regarding the present research, it is crucial for both data pipelines to capture congestion, as well as to identify champions for rival or ally industries and measure the level of commitment those champions have toward those industries. Its unique lobbying database is incredibly extensive and utilizes textual extraction from lobbying reports using machine learning. A weakness of this article as it pertains to the present research, is how to transform the bipartite nature of the current model into a graph format, where path-finding algorithms can be run. Regardless, the current model provides a useful tool for identifying champions and connections across rival industries.
